title: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck Cultural Landscape
summary: A south shore estuarine landscape tied to Native village life, shellfishing, fishing, bay travel, and coastal resource use in Merrick and Massapequa homelands.
address_label: Seaford Creek / Unqua Neck waterways, Seaford-Massapequa area
ancestral_territory_note: Within the wider Merrick/Massapequa south shore cultural landscape; linked here to Merrick Ancestral Land with care about overlapping homelands.
why_this_matters: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck show why tidal waterways and neck lands mattered: they were living landscapes, travel routes, and foodways rather than empty marshes.
introduction_content: An Illustrated History of Massapequa identifies Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck among the coastal places associated with Native habitation and estuarine resource use. These waterways offered access to shellfish, fish, wetlands, and bay travel.1
history_content:
Creeks as connections

The creeks and necks of Seaford and South Oyster Bay linked coastal water with adjacent land. An Illustrated History of Massapequa places Native habitation and resource use within this estuarine setting. Fishing, shellfishing, and travel depended on knowing the relationship between channels, marshes, and the shore.1

Colonial records recast such landscapes as parcels, boundaries, and rights to meadow resources. Massapeoque Meadows explores that change nearby. The Tackapausha Museum and Preserve now carries a Massapequa leader’s name into public environmental education, while the Seaman’s Neck marker connects the waterways with an older route through the land.12
